insights.title: A snack basket by your feeding chair
insights.summary: Food you can reach with one hand.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Feeds can be long and frequent. A small basket next to the place you usually sit means a snack and a drink are always within reach.
Pick things you can open and eat with one hand, and refill the basket when you make a cup of tea.

insights.title: Say yes to meal help
insights.summary: An easy answer to "What can I do?"
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] When friends and family ask how they can help, a meal, a bag of groceries or a tray of something for the freezer is a wonderful answer.
Keeping a short list of favourite meals on your phone makes it easy to say yes.

insights.title: Overnight oats in a jar
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Stir rolled oats and milk together in a jar, add some fruit, close the lid and leave it in the fridge overnight.
In the morning it's ready to eat straight from the jar, with a spoon in one hand.
Full recipe, quantities and variations coming in the Recipes tab.

insights.title: Keep a drink within reach
insights.summary: A full bottle wherever you sit.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] It's easy to forget to drink when your hands are full. Keeping a bottle with a straw or sports cap where you feed makes it simple to sip as you go.

insights.title: Rest counts, too
insights.summary: Lying down for ten minutes is enough.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] You don't need to fill every quiet moment. If the baby is settled and someone is around, it's okay to put your feet up, even for a few minutes.

insights.title: Not feeling like yourself?
insights.summary: You don't have to carry it alone.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] If you have felt sad, anxious, numb or not yourself most days, please talk to your doctor, midwife or health visitor. Asking for help is a strong thing to do.
If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, contact your doctor or local emergency number straight away.

insights.title: Starting with purées
insights.summary: Smooth first, then step by step.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] This guide will be written by a paediatric dietitian. It will cover signs your baby may be ready, starting with smooth purées, and moving on through thicker textures week by week.

insights.title: Freezer cubes, explained
insights.summary: A few hours of prep can stock your freezer for weeks.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Pick some fruits, vegetables and grains. Steam or cook them until soft, then purée.
Serve some fresh, and spoon the rest into ice-cube trays. Once frozen, move the cubes into labelled, dated bags and use them within 3 months.
Later you can mix cubes to make your own combinations. The full guide is in the Planner tab.

insights.title: One meal, two textures
insights.summary: Cook once for the family and baby.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] When you cook a family meal, set aside a plain portion for baby before seasoning, then mash or purée it to the texture they're used to.
Matching family meals for each week of the baby menu are coming soon.

insights.title: Choking: be prepared
insights.summary: Know what to do before you need it.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Choking-hazard guidance by age will be written and reviewed by a paediatric professional. A baby first-aid course is a good way to feel prepared.
If your baby is choking and cannot breathe, cough or cry, call your local emergency number straight away.

insights.title: Share your plate
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Ideas for serving the family meal in toddler-friendly pieces are coming soon, reviewed by a dietitian.

insights.title: Picky phases
insights.summary: You're doing better than you think.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Gentle, practical ideas for picky phases are coming soon, written and reviewed by a paediatric dietitian.
